# Blitz-Recompiler

@difference Extension: `blitz-recompiler` turns an executable made by the original Blitz3D or BlitzPlus compiler into a BlitzLLVM program; the original has no such tool.

`blitz-recompiler` reads the compiled program out of an executable of the original compiler, translates its x86 code to LLVM IR and builds it with `blitzcc`, so that the program runs on the BlitzLLVM runtime. Only use it on programs that you made, or that you may modify.

```sh
blitz-recompiler game.exe -o game-recompiled
blitz-recompiler -S game.exe                      # only write the LLVM IR
blitz-recompiler --userlibs-dir userlibs game.exe # where the .decls files of its user libraries are
```

## User libraries

A program of the original calls the functions of its user libraries (`Decls` files in the `userlibs` directory of the original) through addresses that the original runtime filled in. The executable says which function of which DLL a call is (`_AddInts@8` in `ulib.dll`), but not what the function takes and returns: that was only in the `.decls` file when the program was made. So `blitz-recompiler` reads the [[Userlib-Declarations]] files of the `userlibs` directory (`--userlibs-dir`, `$BLITZLLVM_USERLIBS`, or the directory of the installation) and looks for a declaration of the same library and function for every call. If there is none, the call is not translated: the function that contains it raises a runtime error when the program runs (`--strict` refuses the program instead), and the message names the library function.

The DLLs of the original are 32 bit x86 programs, which a BlitzLLVM program can not load. The libraries have to be built for the system of the program (a `.so`, `.dylib` or `.dll` of the same name, as for source programs), and their functions take what a C compiler gives them there. The recompiled program is a 32 bit program inside, so each call gets a small converter (a thunk) that is made from the declaration:

| Original passes | Library gets |
| --- | --- |
| `Int` (or a smaller number) | the number, extended to 32 bits like C does |
| `Float` | a `float` |
| `String` | a pointer to the characters (a C string) |
| `*` (bank) | the address of the memory of the bank |

Returned `Int`, `Float` and `String` values are converted back the same way; a returned string is copied at once, because the library may reuse its buffer. A declaration that uses a type the original can not pass (`Long`, `Double`, `Half`) is refused, because the program only ever passes 32 bit values. The calling convention is that of the system the program runs on, not `stdcall`.

Not supported: a pointer to a `Type` object as a `*` parameter (only banks), and Windows system DLLs on other systems.
